passages.t: ‘O LORD, remember on behalf of David’: the ark and the promise
passages.happening:
Psalm 132 is the longest of the Songs of Ascents, and it has two halves that answer each other.

In the first half, the people remind God of David's oath. “O LORD, remember on behalf of David all the hardships he endured, how he swore an oath to the LORD” (verses 1 and 2). David vowed not to go to bed “until I find a place for the LORD, a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob” (verse 5). Then the people remember finding the ark and bringing it up. “Let us go to His dwelling place; let us worship at His footstool” (verse 7). “Arise, O LORD, to Your resting place, You and the ark of Your strength” (verse 8). They pray, “For the sake of Your servant David, do not reject Your anointed one” (verse 10).

In the second half, God's own oath is remembered. “The LORD swore an oath to David, a promise He will not revoke: ‘One of your descendants I will place on your throne’” (verse 11). But there is a condition: “If your sons keep My covenant” (verse 12). And God has chosen Zion. “This is My resting place forever and ever” (verse 14). He promises bread for the poor, joy for his people, and a future for David's line: “There I will make a horn grow for David; I have prepared a lamp for My anointed one” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Behind the psalm stand two stories. David brought the ark of the covenant, the gold-covered chest that marked God's presence, up to Jerusalem with shouting and the sound of the ram's horn (2 Samuel 6:15). And God promised David, through the prophet Nathan, a family that would rule (2 Samuel 7). The note on Psalm 120 explains the Songs of Ascents; this one may have been sung in a procession up to the temple.

The ark had stayed for years at Kiriath-jearim, “twenty years in all” (1 Samuel 7:2). ‘The fields of Jaar’ in verse 6 is generally taken as a poetic name for that town, whose name means ‘town of forests’. ‘Ephrathah’ is harder. It is an old name for the area of Bethlehem, David's home town (Micah 5:2). Readers explain it in more than one way.

‘Arise, O LORD’ in verse 8 echoes what Moses said whenever the ark set out in the desert: “Rise up, O LORD!” (Numbers 10:35). The ark was called God's ‘footstool’ (1 Chronicles 28:2), as if God sat enthroned above it.

A horn was a picture of strength. A lamp was a picture of a family line kept alive. God kept “a lamp” for David in Jerusalem even when his sons failed (1 Kings 11:36).

Notice the exchange. David swore he would find God a dwelling. God swore he would give David a dynasty. David wanted to build God a house; God built David a house.
passages.later: The angel told Mary that her son would be given “the throne of His father David” and that “His kingdom will never end!” (Luke 1:32-33). Zechariah praised God who “has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David” (Luke 1:69). At Pentecost Peter said that David knew “that God had promised him on oath that He would place one of his descendants on his throne” (Acts 2:30).
passages.hard: Was God's promise to David unconditional (verse 11) or conditional (verse 12)? Readers hold the two together in different ways. Some stress that God would never take his love from David's line (2 Samuel 7:15). Others stress the condition, since the kings did lose the throne when Babylon took Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC. Many say both are true: a king could lose the blessing by disobeying, but God's purpose for David's line could not fail. Jewish readers hope for a son of David still to come; Christians believe that son is Jesus. The book page's part on the royal psalms sets out both with respect.
passages.asks:
David could not rest until God had a place among his people. What would it mean to care about God's presence that much: in your home, your church, your town?

And the psalm shows God answering a promise with a bigger promise. When you bring God what little you can, he answers with far more than you gave.
